items.text: Free buses are a good idea because cities will have less traffic.
Working from home saves time and money, but many people feel lonely, so I think the advantages are only slightly bigger.

В наши дни дети проводят у экранов по несколько часов в день. На мой взгляд, причин у этого несколько. Во-первых, смартфоны и планшеты стали дешёвыми и есть почти в каждой семье. Во-вторых, родители много работают и часто дают ребёнку телефон, чтобы он был занят. Кроме того, многие школы перешли на электронные учебники и домашние задания онлайн.

Я считаю, что это скорее отрицательная тенденция. Дети меньше двигаются, хуже спят и реже общаются со сверстниками вживую. Конечно, полезные приложения и образовательные видео существуют, но без контроля взрослых ребёнок выбирает игры и развлечения. Поэтому родителям и школам стоит ограничивать экранное время и предлагать детям интересные занятия без гаджетов.

Heute kaufen viele Menschen lieber im Internet ein als in kleinen Geschäften in ihrer Stadt. Dafür gibt es mehrere Gründe. Online-Shops sind rund um die Uhr geöffnet, die Auswahl ist riesig und die Preise sind oft niedriger. Außerdem kann man Bewertungen lesen und Produkte bequem vergleichen, ohne das Haus zu verlassen.

Für die Innenstädte hat diese Entwicklung jedoch ernste Folgen. Viele Läden müssen schließen, weil sie nicht genug Kunden haben, und leere Schaufenster machen die Straßen weniger attraktiv. Dadurch kommen noch weniger Besucher, und auch Cafés und Restaurants verlieren Einnahmen. Meiner Meinung nach sollten Städte deshalb Märkte, Veranstaltungen und niedrige Mieten fördern, damit das Zentrum wieder ein lebendiger Treffpunkt wird.

In this day and age, the issue of whether governments should tax sugary drinks and unhealthy snacks has become a controversial topic that has sparked a heated debate among people from all walks of life. Some people believe it is a good idea, while others hold the opposite view. In this essay, I will discuss both sides of the argument before reaching a reasonable conclusion.

First and foremost, it is undeniable that health is a very important aspect of our lives. As the saying goes, health is wealth. There is no doubt that this issue has both advantages and disadvantages. Every coin has two sides, and this topic is no exception. It goes without saying that this question is relevant to all of us, whether we are young or old. Taking everything into consideration, it can be said that such a tax is a double-edged sword.

On the other hand, it is worth mentioning that people have different opinions about this matter. Some people think one way and other people think another way. Last but not least, it is crucial to bear in mind that every individual is different and has their own needs and preferences in today's fast-paced world.

In conclusion, from my point of view, although there are many advantages and disadvantages, I strongly believe that this is a very complicated issue. It is high time that we paid more attention to this problem, because it plays a vital role in modern society and will continue to be important in the years to come.

It is a well-known fact that crime among young people is one of the most burning issues of the modern world. Nowadays, more and more people are concerned about this phenomenon, and it has become a hot topic of discussion all over the globe. In this essay, I am going to express my point of view on this matter.

To begin with, it goes without saying that young people are the future of every nation. As we all know, crime is a serious problem which affects society in many ways. It is common knowledge that prison sentences are a punishment, and punishment is necessary in our life. From this point of view, it is clear that longer sentences can be a solution to some extent.

Moreover, it should be noted that there are many reasons why young people commit crimes. Needless to say, each case is unique, and the situation can vary from country to country. At the end of the day, this is a question that concerns each and every one of us, and it deserves careful thought. All in all, there are pros and cons to every approach, and this approach is no exception to the rule.

To sum up, all things considered, I would like to say that this is a very complex and multifaceted issue which cannot be solved overnight. Only time will tell whether longer prison sentences are the best way, but one thing is certain: we must do our best to make the world a better place for future generations.

Picture a satellite: not a gleaming rocket on a launch pad, but the small, unglamorous box that tells a farmer in Kenya when the rains will come. Ask most people whether space money should be spent on Earth instead, and they imagine the rocket. They rarely think of the box.

Critics have a fair point, of course. A single mission to Mars can cost billions, and billions buy a great deal of clean water, vaccines and classroom teachers. When children go hungry, gazing at distant planets can look like a luxury, even an insult. If a government must choose between a telescope and a hospital, the hospital should win every time.

Yet the choice is rarely that stark. Space budgets are tiny compared with what most states spend on defence or debt, and much of what they buy comes back to the ground. Weather forecasting, satellite navigation, the monitoring of melting ice and burning forests: all of these rely on technology that exists only because someone, decades ago, was allowed to look up. Even scratch-resistant lenses and portable water filters owe something to engineers who were solving problems in orbit.

So where do I stand? I am not on the launch pad, cheering every expensive flag-planting stunt; I would trim prestige projects ruthlessly. But I would protect the quiet, practical research that turns out to feed, warn and connect people on this planet. Spending on space and solving earthly problems are not rivals. Done wisely, the first is one of the better tools we have for the second.

My grandmother had a word for the smell of rain on dry earth. I have never found it in any dictionary, and when she died, I realised that I might be one of the last people alive who remembered it. That is how languages usually disappear: not with a dramatic ban, but one forgotten word at a time.

Why is this happening? The most obvious reason is economic. Parents want their children to succeed, and success tends to speak the language of the capital city, the university and the internet. A teenager who can hold a job interview in English or Mandarin has opportunities that a fluent speaker of a village language simply does not. Migration accelerates the process, since families who move to cities rarely pass on a language that nobody around them uses. Television, social media and schooling then finish what economics began.

Does it matter? Some argue that fewer languages mean easier communication, and they are not entirely wrong. Yet a language is more than a code for exchanging information. It stores a community's knowledge of plants, weather and history, its jokes and its ways of seeing the world. When it vanishes, that knowledge usually vanishes with it, and no translation can fully bring it back.

I therefore believe that the loss matters a great deal, even if it cannot always be prevented. Recording elderly speakers, teaching local languages alongside national ones and giving them space online are modest steps, but they can keep a language alive long enough for a new generation to decide that it is worth keeping. My grandmother's word deserved at least that chance.
